html:
The House of Habsburg was one of the great ruling families of Europe. From the 1200s to 1918 its members ruled Austria, and at times the Holy Roman Empire, Spain and its American empire, the Low Countries, much of Italy, Hungary and Bohemia.

The family took its name from Habsburg Castle, built in the 1020s in what is now Switzerland. Its old lands there were lost to the Swiss Confederation, which grew out of a pact against Habsburg lords in 1291. Rudolf I, elected king of Germany in 1273, won Austria, which became the family's base. From the 1400s to 1806 the Holy Roman Emperor was almost always a Habsburg.

They grew more by marriage than by war:

  • Maximilian I married the heiress of Burgundy, bringing the Low Countries and the Franche-Comté. He borrowed heavily from the banker Jakob Fugger.
  • His grandson Charles V inherited Spain and its empire as well, the largest realm in Europe.
  • After the battle of Mohács in 1526, Bohemia, Croatia and western Hungary passed to them, and they became Europe's shield against the Ottomans, who besieged Vienna in 1529 and again in 1683; see Siege of Vienna.

Charles split the family into a Spanish and an Austrian line. The Spanish line, weakened by inbreeding, died out in 1700. The Austrian line passed through Maria Theresa to the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, which ruled the Austrian Empire and then Austria-Hungary until defeat in 1918.
